entities.name: PMID:25433681
observations: 2014 qualitative study in BMC Women's Health; semi-structured interviews with 33 women admitted to two major Indian burn units, their families, and 26 doctor, nurse, and police informants; framework analysis.

entities.name: Female burn contexts India
observations: Interviews described accidental burns, attempted suicide, and attempted homicide; assigning cause was difficult amid overlapping poverty, cultural precedent, household conflict, gender-based violence, and alcohol use.
Space constraints, unsafe cooking equipment, and inflammable clothing contributed to accidental burn risk; most burns were initially attributed to accidents.

entities.name: Hospital medicolegal response
observations: Clinicians followed medicolegal procedures and police investigations were relatively rapid, but both groups felt vulnerable; women's reticence, contested and changing accounts, limited forensic evidence, and burdens on clients contributed to pessimism.
The study recommended better documentation, inter-provider communication, and public understanding of burn risks; the authors reported that only a minority of cases led to conviction.
